title: The independent fine-dining industry has negative returns
dek: A 30-year fine-dining restaurateur says independent restaurants have no moat, anyone can copy recipes, complying with labor law costs 5–10% more than competitors, making the industry's overall returns negative.
why: Hear from someone who scaled from a campus coffee shop to fine dining to shared kitchens, laying bare the industry's true cost and profit structure.
who: Entrepreneurs curious about small-business financials, restaurant investors, and anyone wondering why restaurateurs say they don't make money.
skip: The first two minutes of opening pleasantries and self-introduction can be skipped.

points.h: Entrepreneurial success is 20% idea, 80% everything else
points.body: Richard Mott once believed business success was 80% idea; now he reverses it—ideas account for only 20%, with team, environment, and support networks decisive. He cites Home Chef: when approached with what he thought was a bad concept (food ingredients shipped in boxes), the founder convinced him; the company became highly successful.

points.h: Fine-dining restaurants burn through life-years like dogs
points.body: Mott compares independent fine-dining to Broadway productions—closing after three years is normal; surviving 20 is extremely rare. North Pond is approaching 30 years, and he describes restaurants as measuring lifespan ‘in dog years, not human years.’ The business is intensely dependent on word-of-mouth volatility: a positive Chicago Magazine review can book a month solid, but sustaining that momentum proves nearly impossible.

North Pond began when ‘farm-to-table’ was not yet vocabulary. The menu tagline read ‘North Pond·contemporary American seasonal dining’; customers called asking ‘what season do you operate?’ The second chef (also trained in finance at a top school, then retrained as a chef) helped found Green City Market, building a supply network of nearly 100 local farmers, fishermen, and cheese makers that did not exist before.

points.h: No moat, and compliance costs 5–10% more than competitors pay
points.body: Mott regards independent fine-dining as one of the worst industries: no barriers to entry, anyone can open; no patents—copy a new croissant doughnut today, the world copies it tomorrow. The crux: strict compliance with labor, immigration, and overtime law costs 5–10% more than competitors absorb through wage theft, unpaid overtime, and harassment—which has pervaded the sector until #MeToo created consequences. Wharton and SBA data show independent fine-dining's overall returns are negative.

points.h: Some owners are buying restaurants like billionaires buy sports teams
points.body: Mott compares some restaurateurs to wealthy owners buying professional sports franchises—spending $1.2 billion for the Dodgers not for cash flow but to indulge vanity, playing a shell game: five years later, pocket appreciation when selling to the next buyer. When you compete for profit against entrants motivated by ego, the economics are stacked against you.

points.h: Alcohol sales collapsed from 34% of revenue to 24%—and it held the margins
points.body: North Pond's alcohol sales (nearly all wine) held steady at 33–34% of revenue for 28 years, reliable as clockwork; the past 18 months saw a sudden drop to 24%. Mott calls this the industry's largest unspoken crisis, because that vanished 8 percentage points represented the highest-margin segment. Younger customers drink less—partly health-conscious, partly because cannabis and CBD products are replacing alcohol; Lollapalooza recently even featured THC margaritas.

points.h: Price adjustments went from once yearly to four times in 24 months
points.body: The past 3–4 years saw entry-level chef wages rise approximately 30%; food costs saw the steepest increases in the sector. Because restaurants have almost no lag between input costs and menu pricing—ingredients bought this week price this week—what was one adjustment yearly became four in the past 24 months. A two-person dinner with wine pairings now runs approximately $400; North Pond customers no longer come to ‘casually treat themselves on Thursday’ but for milestone moments: a 25th or 50th birthday.

points.h: Shared kitchens: permit Monday, operational Tuesday
points.body: Shared kitchens differ from ghost kitchens—ghost kitchens serve delivery brands and must sit within five minutes' walk of dense population; shared kitchens pool equipment and licensing across small operators. Chicago's shared-kitchen licensing lets new owners get permits Monday and operate Tuesday, while independent restaurants typically wait six months for licensing. Mott's example: three people wanting to launch an ice-cream business found him; pooling one $26,000 industrial ice-cream machine, they could produce 200 gallons daily—scale impossible solo.
